chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Habib ibn Mu'alla al-Kha'thami, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I encountered female slaves in the city and performed my prayer (while in a state of major impurity, without performing ghusl).' He said: 'As for the one who intends to buy them, there is no harm in it. And as for the one who does not intend to buy them, I dislike it.'

key_terms.فَأَمْذَيْتُ: and I performed my prayer (without ghusl)
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِهِ بَأْسٌ: there is no harm in it

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on performing prayer after sexual intercourse with a female slave one intends to keep versus one one does not intend to keep?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between two scenarios regarding the ritual purity (ghusl) of a man after sexual intercourse with a female slave: if he intends to purchase her, the act is not considered problematic for prayer, but if he does not intend to keep her, he is advised to perform ghusl. This ruling highlights the jurisprudential nuance in Shia fiqh where the intention of ownership or retention affects the ritual status, reflecting the social and economic context of slavery in early Islamic society. The hadith is found in the chapter on rentals and transactions (Bab al-Ijarat), linking personal ritual purity to broader commercial and social contracts.
